blocks.text: Capture a business rule as a small object that answers yes or no for a candidate, and combine rules with and, or and not.

A **specification** has one question: `isSatisfiedBy(candidate)`. Simple rules are named and unit-tested alone. **Combinators** build complex rules from them, so `eligible = adult.and(solvent).and(notDefaulted.not())` reads like the requirement. The same rule can validate, filter and select.
In Java, a specification is a `Predicate` with domain names. Write a dedicated type when rules need names, reuse or translation to queries.

walkthrough.note: The interface has one abstract method; `and`, `or` and `not` are default methods returning new specs. Composition is closed: combining specs yields a spec.
Each leaf rule is a tiny record with one condition and a name from the business vocabulary. Parameters live in the record.
Rules combine into the requirement exactly as a product owner would phrase it. None of the leaves changed.
The composed rule is applied to each applicant. The caller sees a single `isSatisfiedBy` and doesn't care how complex the rule is.

blocks.text: Promotion eligibility rules edited by the marketing team.

Campaigns say: customers who spent over 200 in the last year, are not in a blocked region, and either joined before 2024 or have a referral. Each condition is a specification with its own test. A campaign is assembled from configuration, and the same specification both filters the mailing list and checks eligibility at checkout.
Payoff: marketing changes a campaign by recombining tested rules, and mailing and checkout can't disagree.

lists.title: Use when
items: Rules are numerous, change often, and are combined in many ways.
One rule must serve validation, filtering and query building.
Business experts need rules named in the domain's vocabulary.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: There are two fixed conditions: an `if` is clearer.
A plain `Predicate` with a lambda already says it well.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Rules that perform I/O inside `isSatisfiedBy`, making them slow and untestable.
In-memory filtering of huge sets when the rule should become a database query.
Deep combinator chains that hide a rule's meaning; name the combined spec.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: Specs wrapping single trivial comparisons that appear once.
A generic spec framework before any rule is duplicated.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Sealed interfaces plus records make an inspectable rule tree that can be translated to SQL.

rows.difference: Both are small interchangeable objects with one method. A strategy computes a result to use; a specification returns a boolean and is designed to be combined.
Composite specs are a Composite: and, or and not treat single and combined rules uniformly.
Interpreter models a rule language with its own grammar and parser. A specification is a lighter, code-level rule combinator.
A chain lets the first handler that accepts act. A specification composes all conditions into one verdict.
A repository can accept a specification as its query criteria, so the rule drives both memory and database filtering.

template: interface Spec<T> { boolean isSatisfiedBy(T t); default Spec<T> and(Spec<T> o) { return t -> isSatisfiedBy(t) && o.isSatisfiedBy(t); } }
record Applicant(String n, int a, int i, boolean d) {}
record AtLeastAge(int y) implements Spec<Applicant> { public boolean isSatisfiedBy(Applicant a) { return a.a() >= y; } }
record MinIncome(int m) implements Spec<Applicant> { public boolean isSatisfiedBy(Applicant a) { return a.i() >= m; } }

exercises.prompt: Explain the Specification pattern: what a spec is, how rules combine, and when a plain Predicate is enough.

modelAnswer.text: A specification is an object that decides whether a candidate satisfies one business rule. Small named specs combine through and, or and not into larger rules, and can be reused for validation, filtering and query building. A plain Predicate is enough when rules are few, unshared and need no names or translation to queries.

keyPoints: Named leaf rules, each tested alone
Reused for validation, filtering and queries
Predicate suffices for simple, local rules
